sources.title: AI That Works #33: No Vibes Allowed: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer
sources.note: Full transcript read (3885 lines). Vaibhav drives, Dex navigates; three CodeLayer features (AI titles, Obsidian opener, context-switch summaries). The README in the sources folder is only a stub (overview + whiteboard links), read in full (~90 words).

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the less context you use, the better results you get
cards.claim: Workflow is built on frequent intentional compaction: research produces a baked understanding so planning happens in the sweet spot of a fresh, small context window.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as the basic idea of the research/plan/implement workflow; demonstrated live on a BAML Rust feature (no measurement).
cards.landing: Phase routine in ship plan section 0 (one phase per new chat); already largely present
cards.inventory_ref: (B) June to December 2025 - 2025-10-16 'No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents'

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we'll start a new context window for this one since we've already used about 30%
cards.claim: Once the spec is correct, throw away the context spent perfecting it and reseed a new window with only the final spec, rather than carrying the history of edits.
cards.evidence_detail: Done live at ~30% usage; the co-host explains it is not about cache but about the model not being confused by old vs new spec.
cards.landing: Phase routine: new chat per phase seeded from the artifact (plan @ sha), not from conversation history

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I try to keep the context under 40%.
cards.claim: Dex's practical working budget is under 40% of the window, tolerating 40-50% only if the task is nearly finished, and being aggressive otherwise (restarting at ~60%).
cards.evidence_detail: Stated while live coding; later in the same session he restarts at 63% and complains of 'context anxiety' near 60%.
cards.landing: A context-budget line in the phase routine or closing message ('percent of window used at handoff')

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You have to read this stuff.
cards.claim: The workflow is not a magic prompt; the human must read the diff and research/plan documents, and the leverage comes from reading higher-level artifacts.
cards.evidence_detail: Said right after opening the diff of the model's spec edit; co-host adds that not reading code is why his own vibe-coding got worse.
cards.landing: Owner one-page view / reviewer step: what a human must actually read

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'm looking for approximate fuzzy matching
cards.claim: Reviewing a research doc means checking file:line references are roughly right with an expert in the codebase present; chasing 100% correctness has diminishing returns, and the expert adds omissions the model missed.
cards.evidence_detail: Live: the BAML expert caught a missed file (orchestrator/stream.rs), the stream-only nature of idle timeout, and irrelevant publishing timeouts.
cards.landing: Cold-resume trial / research artifact review: someone who knows the repo skims for omissions, not correctness

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: of which parts of the system are relevant can tank your entire project
cards.claim: Errors compound upward: a bad line of code is one bad line, a bad plan step is a hundred, and a research misunderstanding of what is relevant sinks the project, so review effort belongs on research and plan.
cards.evidence_detail: Aside during plan reading; framed as the reason to read research/plan carefully.
cards.landing: Reviewer weighting: refute plan and research artifacts first

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The plan gives you 10x leverage. The research gives you 100x leverage.
cards.claim: Do not delegate spec writing to the model too; accept being 100x faster rather than reaching for 1000x, because past that returns diminish and some manual reading/pruning is still worth it.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative multipliers, no data.
cards.landing: Where the human stays in the loop: spec/ticket authoring and artifact pruning

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: make sure you don't get into the details of how to make an implementation plan
cards.claim: The research prompt is documentation-only: map relevant code, tests, integration tests and codegen, explicitly not plan or solve, so the next fresh agent starts from facts.
cards.evidence_detail: Prompt typed live; the research prompt itself is described as 'its only job is to document and explain' with parallel sub-agents and front-matter.
cards.landing: Research step / skill wording in the phase routine

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the code base locator, its job is to document the code base
cards.claim: A small set of single-purpose sub-agents (locator = super grep, analyzer = trace data flow, pattern finder) is invoked by the research prompt, and can also be steered to by hand for pinpoint questions instead of writing a new research doc.
cards.evidence_detail: Agent definitions shown from the humanlayer repo; 'use code base pattern finder' used live to find how errors and Python tests are written.
cards.landing: .claude/agents/ (extends the single Haiku locator; add analyzer and pattern-finder roles)

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're setting the trajectory to be a little bit more towards your few-shot prompting
cards.claim: Invoke the plan command with no arguments so the first turns are a user/agent back-and-forth, which makes the model more likely to ask questions and outline phases instead of just calling tools until done.
cards.evidence_detail: Explained as trajectory few-shotting; co-host called it a micro-optimisation and Dex said experience with these prompts would convince him.
cards.landing: Plan step of the phase routine (how the plan session is opened)

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: really focus on what is the incrementally testable thing
cards.claim: Design plan phases around what can be run and verified at the end of each phase; if a verification cannot happen until phase three, merge those phases, and split phases that are too meaty.
cards.evidence_detail: Applied live: phase one was split into parsing then client creation, error definitions moved before the timeout implementation.
cards.landing: Plan template: each phase names its runnable check

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the smaller you can make your phases, the more you can
cards.claim: Smaller phases let you learn from the first implementation and revise the rest of the plan, and each phase should compile or test on its own.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex moved composite-client work to its own later phase because he did not know how it would work; plans were revised twice mid-session.
cards.landing: Phase sizing guidance in the ship plan

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if it has existing check marks, trust that that's done
cards.claim: The implement prompt checks off plan items as it goes and, on resume, trusts existing check marks, starting from the first unchecked item and re-verifying earlier work only if something looks off.
cards.evidence_detail: Shown live; speaker of this specific sentence is ambiguous in captions (Dex or Vaibhav) but it is Dex's prompt set.
cards.landing: Plan checkbox convention and resume rule for a new session picking up mid-plan; the cold-resume trial

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: somewhere in between clear and compact
cards.claim: At the limit, have the model write a handoff prompt that starts with the implement command and a plan-file reference, then launch the next session from it via a CLI; Dex preferred this to the auto-compaction summary.
cards.evidence_detail: Done live after auto-compaction was about to fire; he says 'it already compacted itself ... we're still going to do a handoff and start over'.
cards.landing: Handoff-prompt convention for the end of a phase/session (closing message could be a launchable prompt)

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: LLMs are bad at judging things, if you ask me
cards.claim: Better tests give the model an objective measure; LLMs are poor judges but good at reading errors and fixing them, so do not obsess over a perfect plan, only a good-enough one that lets test errors drive the fix.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion offered while the model iterated on cargo test failures.
cards.landing: Verifier design: prefer executable checks over judge-style review; reviewer cites test output

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you almost never want that
cards.claim: Keeping all historical research and plans visible to the model is usually wrong; give the model all artifacts for the current ticket only, plus a few hand-manicured 'golden research' files (for example how tests work) that are always findable.
cards.evidence_detail: 'In the past we kept all historical research and plans ... what I'm finding more and more is you almost never want that.' Vaibhav says he never saves them in the repo at all.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store design: scope retrieval per task; a small curated always-available set instead of everything

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the research basically gives you on-demand up-to-date code-based documentation
cards.claim: Dex is lukewarm on agent-maintained code documentation for other developers because when everyone ships a thousand lines every couple of days it goes stale; on-demand research (about 10 minutes) replaces it.
cards.evidence_detail: Claim made when asked whether spec and code stay connected; no data.
cards.landing: Argues against persistent generated docs in the knowledge-store pilot; favours regenerate-on-demand research

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: move it into your infrastructure
cards.claim: Whenever you find you always want the model to do something one way (for example run parser tests with update-expect, or build primitives before streaming before composites), move it into the commands and agents rather than re-typing it each plan.
cards.evidence_detail: Said while adding guidance to the create-plan command; co-host would not put such task-specific text in CLAUDE.md and suggested prompt snippets.
cards.landing: Skills / command files; also supports keeping task-specific rules out of CLAUDE.md

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I have a global cloud ND that steers it to make
cards.claim: A stale global CLAUDE.md instruction (use make) kept overriding the plan's own test commands in a repo that does not use make, and he had to remove it.
cards.evidence_detail: Happened twice live ('Read the damn plan, you nerd'); he later says 'this shouldn't be in my global thing anyways'.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md audit: always-loaded rules can silently conflict with phase-specific plan commands

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The first thing in your path should be something else.
cards.claim: Prevent a wrong-tool habit deterministically by shadowing the binary (python shimmed to echo 'use uv') rather than relying on the model to follow an instruction.
cards.evidence_detail: Co-host describes Dex's shim; Dex confirms the principle but had to remove it; also recounts a friend whose agent ran rm -rf on a tilde directory.
cards.landing: Re-opens the skipped hooks idea (PATH shim or PreToolUse hook as a deterministic enforcement channel)

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The best engineers I know like they don't use evals.
cards.claim: The best engineers rely on judgment from about 70 hours a week with the model rather than evals; the best investment is a good vibe-checker in your own head.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says it once; the co-host extends it ('most prompting is all vibes'); no data.
cards.landing: Counter to building a measurement pipeline (the skipped item); supports owner judgment as the check

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the model will just keep rewriting it with the new stuff
cards.claim: Hand-editing a plan while another session is still writing it fails: the model overwrites the edit and re-introduces the removed content, so edits go through the model or after it finishes.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed live (a 10-minute max he removed came back); co-host notes he uses a prompt saying 'I sometimes make edits you don't have'.
cards.landing: Plan-file ownership rule in the phase routine (single writer at a time)

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we're paralyzing between phase one and also iterating on phase two
cards.claim: Implement phase N in one session while refining the plan for phase N+1 in another, because each reviewed artifact has the same shape and you do not pay full context-switch cost.
cards.evidence_detail: Done live; he also says parallel tasks work because everything you review is shaped the same.
cards.landing: Workflow orchestration: pipeline plan-review ahead of implementation

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you should almost always be using Opus
cards.claim: For research over a large complex codebase use the strongest model and cancel a run on a weaker one; paying more avoids the cost of restarting after a wrong result.
cards.evidence_detail: Cancelled a Sonnet research run and restarted on Opus; co-host argues speed and cheaper models are fine for most work, so the two disagree on routing.
cards.landing: Effort/model routing for verifiers and researchers (note: Oct 2025 models, pre-dates the xhigh-vs-medium report)

cards.source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: my most my most important resource is my time
cards.claim: Skip slow, low-risk checks (run the TypeScript tests only at the very end) when a cheaper proxy such as Python compiling is a good predictor, optimising for human time while still guaranteeing the full run happens eventually.
cards.evidence_detail: Said when choosing which tests the plan's verification step should run.
cards.landing: Verification step tiering (cheap checks per phase, full suite before close)

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you don't come with opinions, the model will not
cards.claim: You cannot outsource the thinking: if you know what you want (phase order, structure), state it; Dex overrode a model-written plan with his own phase order rather than iterating on it.
cards.evidence_detail: Said when the co-host wanted to lean on the model more; Dex ties it to 12-factor: put the known workflow in deterministic code and let the model write code, tests and fixes.
cards.landing: Principle for plan review: the human supplies phase order and unknowns
cards.inventory_ref: (A4) CodeLayer; (B) June to December 2025 - 'Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer'

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: put your biggest unknowns as the first phase
cards.claim: Order plan phases to retire the biggest unknown first (here: can the Haiku call be invoked and pulled through), before schema and wiring work.
cards.evidence_detail: Said while explaining why the model's draft plan was wrong; the first phase was then validated by an integration test.
cards.landing: Plan template: risk-first phase ordering

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: sprinting to as quickly as possible get to wired all the way through
cards.claim: Models plan horizontally (database, service, API, front end) so nothing is testable until phase three; steer to vertical slices wired end-to-end early, and fix the create-plan prompt to say so.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed in the draft plan: 'they're very horizontal ... only by the end of phase three can you run a curl'; says create-plan needs updating.
cards.landing: Plan template / skill: vertical-slice requirement

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you really want to iterate on the phases before you go write the file
cards.claim: Make the model propose open questions and a phase outline before it writes the plan, since a few hundred tokens of outline are cheap to iterate whereas the written plan consumes much of the useful window.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed the model writing the file before outline review, leaving Dex 'in the dumb zone or needing to rebuild all that context'.
cards.landing: Plan step: outline gate before the plan document

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: eat the like 8% of the context window that is required
cards.claim: Writing a ~600-line plan document costs about 8% of the context window, so steer as much as possible before it is written.
cards.evidence_detail: Single stated figure, 'this 600 line markdown document'; not measured in an experiment.
cards.landing: Context budget accounting per phase

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: even Opus 4.1 would skip steps all the time.
cards.claim: Models skip the interactive steps of a prompt even when instructed; reinforce the key orders in the user message ('magic words') such as 'work back and forth with me, start with open questions, show the phase outline before writing the plan'.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says he has done 'thousands of these' and knows to notice a skipped questions step; novices will not notice; also says Opus 4.5 sometimes skips steps.
cards.landing: Phase-routine opening prompt; relates to self-reported compliance (skips are invisible to novices)

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You want a very easy way to convince yourself that the code itself is correct.
cards.claim: Each phase needs a cheap human-checkable proof of correctness (shell command, integration test, one-off Go main) so the human does not have to read the logic; otherwise leverage is lost.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued against the co-host's preference for reading code; 'I want to be able to hit that endpoint with a curl and it works'.
cards.landing: Per-phase verification line in the plan; reviewer asks for the proof, not the diff

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models are not good at evaluating whether code is correct
cards.claim: Do not rely on the model (or on reading every line) to establish correctness; give it something validatable that is not model judgment.
cards.evidence_detail: Short assertion during the testing debate; consistent with the later SlopCodeBench-era claims.
cards.landing: Against review-agent-only verification; supports executable proof requirements

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I guarantee it's going to like mock the things that we care about.
cards.claim: Agent-written unit tests for a phase tend to mock the exact integration (here the CLI call) that matters; require a real, un-mocked integration test for the risky part.
cards.evidence_detail: Prediction before reading the model's tests; he then judged the generated tests not useful.
cards.landing: Reviewer checklist: fail-before/pass-after tests must hit the real boundary

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: have a little proof of concept script before you go into planning
cards.claim: Run a throwaway proof-of-concept (a shell one-liner or script) before planning, and treat reverse-engineering a black box as a missing stage of research.
cards.evidence_detail: Used to prove the Claude CLI could do a one-off text-in/text-out call and to probe whether Obsidian opens non-vault files; he says it is not yet baked into the methodology.
cards.landing: Research step: optional PoC for unknown external behaviour (relevant to Railway/Expo/Supabase behaviour)

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you want to keep the model objective as long as possible
cards.claim: Keep research objective (how the system works today) separate from how it will work; models are good at explaining and bad at evaluating, and research questions should be things not discoverable from code, not implementation questions.
cards.evidence_detail: A/B of two research runs (with and without the spec in the prompt): the no-spec run produced objective questions, the other produced implementation choices; models pick their first idea when implementation leaks in.
cards.landing: Research prompt design; separation of fact-finding from planning

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: tell it the parts of the codebase that are going to matter
cards.claim: In research, tell the agent which areas matter without telling it what you are building; stash the implementation ask in a text file for the planning step.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's stated practice, contrasted live with the co-host's spec-in-research approach; the co-host accepts it is a different style.
cards.landing: Research/plan hand-off format in the phase routine

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: give me a bunch of boolean flags about like what is true
cards.claim: Do not ask a model for a 1-10 score of how good something is; ask for boolean facts about the thing and let deterministic code decide.
cards.evidence_detail: Recalled from an earlier AITW email-classification episode; applied here to why research should stay descriptive.
cards.landing: Verdict schema for refuters and critics: structured true/false findings, verdict computed in code

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: doing the exact same work, but you're using smaller context windows to do the work
cards.claim: A phase-implement command moves implementation into a sub-agent per phase that tests and validates, then reports to the parent which checks and asks for manual validation; all phases can run in one parent session using smaller windows.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex insisted on it for a small change and argued 'worst case I waste five minutes'; the co-host's tests of it were mixed. Calls it a new CodeLayer capability.
cards.landing: Workflow script: parent orchestrator with per-phase worker sub-agents; skill for phase implement

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it dictates the amount of context engineering that you have to do
cards.claim: Task size and difficulty dictate how much context engineering to apply; the only way to calibrate is to over- and under-do it repeatedly, and Dex tells people to try things they think will not work.
cards.evidence_detail: Repeated across the stream (also 'binary search on either side'); co-host regularly pushes to 70% and the two disagree.
cards.landing: Effort routing: scale process weight to task size; small changes skip the full routine

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: pick a dimension and then eval across that dimension for your own intuition
cards.claim: Vary one dimension at a time (tools, amount of context engineering, repos) over a week and compare, locking the others; reset expectations when a new model ships.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex describes rotating dimensions weekly ('still all vibes, but intentional'); the co-host instead snaps between workflows at each model release.
cards.landing: A routing experiment protocol (medium vs xhigh) rather than a one-off switch

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how do you edit a plan in flight when you realize something was wrong
cards.claim: Open problem: how to re-steer a plan (back out, edit) when a defect is discovered after three phases of implementation; Dex's workaround was to fork back and give very specific instructions.
cards.evidence_detail: Arose when the model silently edited both sides of the OpenAPI contract and then tried regenerating types needing Docker.
cards.landing: Decisions journal / plan-amendment rule in the draft PR; re-plan procedure

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: figure out the contract between the front end and the back end
cards.claim: Define the front/back contract, mock the backend side, get the front end right visually, then implement the backend, so debugging has a visual reference and the contract is known correct.
cards.evidence_detail: Offered as an alternative tactic after the plan's phase order was discussed; not tried on stream.
cards.landing: Plan tactic for mobile/web vs backend slices (technician-app and src/ against FastAPI schemas)

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: It'll just like edit both sides of the contract which is like very wrong.
cards.claim: Agents sometimes edit the generated artifact and its consumer instead of the source contract (OpenAPI schema) so it technically works but is wrong; check that the contract source changed.
cards.evidence_detail: Confirmed on stream: the session-title event type was added but the OpenAPI spec was not updated, so the new field never reached the client.
cards.landing: Reviewer checklist item (schemas.py/models vs migration, API schema vs clients; drift checks already in CI)

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: actually sharing your prod database for your stable version
cards.claim: A dev build of the app was silently sharing the stable version's database and daemon; separate the dev database path and verify which store a test hits before trusting results.
cards.evidence_detail: Debugging detour of about 10 minutes; worktrees also lacked the untracked .env, so dev environments must be copied in.
cards.landing: Worktree/environment setup checklist for phases; do not let verification touch shared state

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: controll X and fork it and just add that to your original instructions
cards.claim: Rather than interrupting a running session with a correction, fork the conversation at an earlier turn and amend the original instructions; he also forks back to before the plan was written.
cards.evidence_detail: Used repeatedly in the stream (fork command in CodeLayer) to retry with better wording without paying for the noisy branch.
cards.landing: Context forking practice (his later 2026 forking post is by Kyle); fits correction-by-rewind in a phase

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: maybe that's a side effect of the fact that you're constantly pushing the context window
cards.claim: Dex speculates that the co-host's distrust of plan execution may result from routinely running sessions to 70% of the window.
cards.evidence_detail: Hypothesis only; the co-host defended long contexts ('people can push context windows further than they think').
cards.landing: Context-budget policy debate (who is right is unmeasured)

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: one or two plan sessions and then one or two implementation sessions
cards.claim: The natural unit of work is a task (one ticket or issue) with one or two research, plan and implementation sessions each, which the tool should group, rather than a vague 'project'.
cards.evidence_detail: Product-design remark answering a viewer; reflects how his team shapes sessions.
cards.landing: Ticket-per-phase mapping; how sessions are named and grouped in the PR

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there's a lot of like oral tradition that goes into this stuff
cards.claim: The method relies on unwritten instinct, so the product should add guard rails (fewer foot-guns) that work even for people without LLM intuition.
cards.evidence_detail: Said while explaining CodeLayer's design aim; no evidence on whether it works.
cards.landing: Encode tacit habits as prompts/skills/checks so a fresh agent (cold-resume trial) does not depend on them

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: used like thousands of tokens for a thing you could have told the model
cards.claim: Pasting a screenshot to describe a UI change costs thousands of tokens when a sentence would do.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's criticism of the co-host pasting an image into the prompt; the co-host replied images are faster and help UI.
cards.landing: Context-hygiene tip for prompts

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: all of these sub agents run with sonnet
cards.claim: Research sub-agents are hard-coded to a cheaper model in the agent header while the parent runs the stronger model, and the sub-agent prompt can be inspected to verify what was passed.
cards.evidence_detail: Shown by opening the sub-agent tool call; he also notes the model sometimes picks Haiku itself for a sub-agent.
cards.landing: .claude/agents/ frontmatter model field; effort routing per agent

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: so there's no git or codebase context clouding the system prompt
cards.claim: For a one-off model call (title generation) run it with a small model, an overridden system prompt, and in a temp directory so no repo context contaminates it, and keep it out of the normal tracked-session path.
cards.evidence_detail: Design spec dictated for the title feature; the integration test ran it via the user's subscription rather than an API key.
cards.landing: Pattern for cheap sub-calls (e.g. a verifier that starts with no repo context beyond the claim and the diff)

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: forget to check the like actual testing steps
cards.claim: Everyone, including Dex, forgets to run the plan's manual testing steps; he walks the co-host through the manual verification that the implementation output itself stated.
cards.evidence_detail: Live: the implementation report listed 'start the daemon and verify migration applies'; the co-host skipped it and the new column was missing until a dev-environment fix.
cards.landing: Self-reported compliance gap: human-run steps in the plan are the most-skipped; make them explicit in the closing message

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: This took the plan for me from like 70% to 90%.
cards.claim: Reading and steering a plan until it is about 90% right is enough; do not micromanage it, and time spent reading plans shrinks as you get reps.
cards.evidence_detail: Subjective percentages, stated after one round of feedback on the phase order.
cards.landing: Plan-review stopping rule (diminishing returns)

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You got to let the tooling do the deterministic things
cards.claim: Let the AI do what it is good at, let tooling do the deterministic things you want every time, and leave the human the high-leverage thinking, design and architecture; e.g. auto-inject a 'yes' when the model re-asks for an obvious go-ahead.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex states the principle; the auto-yes idea was the co-host's and Dex agreed.
cards.landing: Hooks/scripts for routine steps (re-opens skipped hooks idea) and saved workflows

cards.source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: the diff is like verifiably true
cards.claim: To build a similar feature, hand the model the git diff/commit of an earlier small feature as the example instead of the plan, since the diff is verifiably what was done; teams keep generalizable sample PRs for this.
cards.evidence_detail: Co-host proposed it; Dex agreed it gives better results for least effort and says his team does it all the time.
cards.landing: Worked-example library of reference diffs in the repo or skills

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I think most people skip is actually what I call like program design
cards.claim: Beyond product and architecture, the step most people skip is program design: decide before the agent runs the decisions it would make badly (file placement, types and signatures, call stack), because it will make choices you may not like.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex demos a PRD and architecture session (43k tokens) that precedes program design; Ondrej sells a bundle of his program-design system.
cards.landing: Plan template with product, architecture, program-design and vertical-slice sections (QRSPI-like)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - 2026-08-07 David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I personally don't think this works and this was like kind of my epiphany
cards.claim: A lights-off factory where nobody reads the code does not work; you can lose touch with the codebase and later hit a bug the models cannot fix.
cards.evidence_detail: Based on Dex's own July 2025 experience; stated as a thesis with odds, not data.
cards.landing: Owner/human reading requirement; limits on removing human review

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we were miserable reading through a bunch of like slop code trying to figure out
cards.claim: In July 2025 the team reviewed plans and tickets but not code; on hitting a bug they spent weeks in slop while shipping a buggy desktop app, which is why they threw out the lights-off approach.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's account; his thesis is the odds of this happening are much higher than not if you stop reading code.
cards.landing: Cautionary evidence for the harness: plan review alone is insufficient

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: it'll quiz you on like what is the current state of the code base
cards.claim: Keep the human in charge by having the agent educate and quiz them (HTML visualizations, multiple choice, mermaid diagrams) and by slowing down on purpose when you lose your grip; Dex prototyped a quiz-while-the-agent-works feature.
cards.evidence_detail: Ondrej raised quizzes and visualizations; Dex said they built a prototype and may bring it back.
cards.landing: Closing message or owner view that tests understanding (and show-me style visuals)

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The whole like concept here is like back pressure, right?
cards.claim: Give the model deterministic feedback it can optimise against (a business metric such as conversion, test results), with LLM judges acceptable but weaker; tie work to a number that matters.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated while discussing measurable outcomes and A/B experiments that an agent checks daily.
cards.landing: Output backpressure scripts and verifier design

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: other
cards.quote: If you can tell it a measurable output, the agent will move mountains for you.
cards.claim: A measurable output target makes agents effective (the slash-goal / auto-research pattern).
cards.evidence_detail: Ondrej's line; Dex agrees and compares it to auto-research, a kernel-speed target.
cards.landing: Phase success criteria expressed as measurable checks

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't wake up to an alert, I wake up to a pull request
cards.claim: Route incidents and triaged support tickets straight into the factory so alarms produce pull requests, and even 30-50% of work automated roughly doubles throughput.
cards.evidence_detail: Arithmetic illustration, not measured; Ondrej says he does it with a cheap model reviewing every uptime incident.
cards.landing: Scheduled/triggered agents against Sentry or deploy alerts (outside the 40-phase plan)

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: spend an hour up front to save hours in the review time
cards.claim: Teams invested up-front alignment meetings to save review time; agents make building fast but review stays the bottleneck, so spend effort up front (product, architecture, design) to shrink review.
cards.evidence_detail: His pre-AI and post-AI software-factory framing; no data.
cards.landing: Ship plan rationale: front-load plan review to cut PR review

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Well, we threw Codex and Opus at it
cards.claim: Cross-model agentic review that finds and fixes the small stuff raises trust but does not remove the review bottleneck for the code that matters.
cards.evidence_detail: Example: both models found ten issues each, all fixed, trust increased.
cards.landing: Reviewer design: different model for review than for authoring

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if the model knew what good code looked like, then it would be able
cards.claim: Review agents raise the floor (catch small stuff) but cannot fix slop: if a model could tell good code from bad it would write good code to begin with, since the reviewer and author are the same models.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says he cannot quite prove it but 'everybody I know has this vibe'; says model quality judges can only go so far.
cards.landing: Limits of the Opus reviewer per PR: it catches mechanical defects, not design quality

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: maintainability has no fast oracle
cards.claim: RL cannot easily reward maintainability because bad architecture shows up in weeks or months and cannot be backpropagated, while tests give an oracle in seconds; so models are tuned to pass tests, not to write maintainable code.
cards.evidence_detail: Explained with a diagram of RL traces scored on tests, conciseness and external verification; no experiment shown here.
cards.landing: Rationale for human/design gates beyond tests

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: this problem does not penalize the model for writing slop
cards.claim: A high SWE-bench-style score does not show the model writes maintainable code, because the grader only checks that hidden tests pass and nothing penalises bad design.
cards.evidence_detail: Walks through a small SWE-bench Multilingual task (a ~100-200 line golden patch); notes possible training contamination.
cards.landing: Skepticism toward benchmark claims when choosing models/effort

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have a road map of 20 features and the model doesn't know any
cards.claim: A trustworthy benchmark would feed the model features one at a time without revealing the roadmap, to test whether code stays easy to change, unlike one-shot problems that tell the model the whole task.
cards.evidence_detail: Proposed benchmark design (the idea behind his SlopCodeBench work); no result here.
cards.landing: Basis for evaluating models/effort on multi-step evolution, not single tasks

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: let's remove the model's patch and run the test against the pre-patch code
cards.claim: A check that the model's own tests fail on the code before the patch exposes tests that test nothing; a new benchmark (Cognition's) does this plus a rules-based LLM quality judge and a functional-equivalence judge against a golden patch.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex describes the benchmark and says it points in the right direction though it does not solve slop; endorses the test-must-fail-before idea.
cards.landing: Reviewer's fail-before/pass-after requirement; a script that runs new tests against the base commit

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: keep it very focused and say like say yes or no, did it follow all the rules
cards.claim: LLM quality judges are not deterministic but a focused yes/no rule-following check gives more stable scoring than just test passing; still limited.
cards.evidence_detail: Commentary on the Cognition judge design.
cards.landing: Refuter prompt shape: one rule per question, yes/no, verdict defaults refuted

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: basically comments out test to get them to pass
cards.claim: Agents sometimes comment out tests to make them pass, so a grader keeps the agent's changes to tests visible and runs the original tests; recurring slop patterns (catch-log-rethrow, weird type casts) are what the gaming looks like.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says he is sure the host has seen it; names JSON.parse try/catch-and-log and type casts as typical slop.
cards.landing: Lint/CI rules for slop patterns; reviewer checks test files for weakened assertions

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models love to build things in a horizontal way
cards.claim: Vertical slices (tracer bullets): get a thin path working end to end first, then add logic and error handling; Dex has never seen a model do this unprompted, so the human specifies the order so every step is testable.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites Matt Pocock and a January chat; compares to how he built before AI.
cards.landing: Plan template; slice-ordering rule in the ship plan

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Let me re-steer it now when it's cheap
cards.claim: Peek at the code after the first two steps of a vertical slice and re-steer then, because steering a thousand-line result later is expensive.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued with no data.
cards.landing: Early-checkpoint rule in the phase routine

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can make a lot of these decisions in a very context cheap way
cards.claim: Make architecture and design decisions in a short session (43k tokens had settled endpoints, flow, files) so you get the model's best reasoning before long-context degradation, and before it is biased by what it already wrote.
cards.evidence_detail: Shown with a live session at 43,000 tokens; also says that once hundreds of lines exist, changes are harder because the context is already biased.
cards.landing: Plan sessions kept short and separate from implementation sessions

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We just define the types and the method signatures
cards.claim: Plans show human-scannable code blocks of types and method signatures (not implementations) so a reviewer can quickly judge right or wrong.
cards.evidence_detail: Prompting practice at HumanLayer.
cards.landing: Plan format guideline

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Here's what the tests are going to look like and here's what the call stack
cards.claim: Plans should end with what the tests will look like and the expected call stack (Dylan Mulroy, Cloudflare), which Dex calls very good.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex cites a recent tweet; adopted into his program-design step.
cards.landing: Plan template end section: tests and call stack

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: write the blog post before you build the feature
cards.claim: Write the user-facing explanation (Amazon working backwards) plus a PRD with success measure and plain-HTML mockups before any architecture; 20 minutes of this raises the odds the agent ships without hand polish.
cards.evidence_detail: Shows his own PRD for bringing custom workflows into the product; no tech in it.
cards.landing: Optional product-spec stage before planning for UI-affecting phases

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there are times to vibe code
cards.claim: The program-design process is for teams of about five or more engineers with paying customers; pre-product-market-fit startups should vibe code and test the market, where the process is overkill.
cards.evidence_detail: Scope limit he states himself (regulated clients: a mistake can mean a million-dollar fine).
cards.landing: Effort routing by risk: FixFlow has real money and users so full routine applies

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: make the environment like close as possible to what the model is good at
cards.claim: Put plans, designs and external context into the file system (read, write, edit, grep, bash) with hooks that sync it, instead of instructions on how to reach context via MCP.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes his product design; says it makes context retrieval efficient.
cards.landing: Repo-resident decision/plan artifacts; knowledge-store as plain files

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: but it doesn't cost inference
cards.claim: Instructions telling the model how to fetch context waste attention; fetch it deterministically with a session-start hook (e.g. last 10 Sentry issues) which costs CPU, not inference, and save inference for reasoning.
cards.evidence_detail: Example given; no measurement.
cards.landing: Re-opens the skipped hooks decision: SessionStart hook injecting repo state; shortens CLAUDE.md

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: other
cards.quote: just like /docs/adr and document all ADRs explicitly
cards.claim: Keep ADRs and a docs/external folder (env var names, payment setup, test emails, who to contact) in the repo as markdown so models can find non-code facts.
cards.evidence_detail: Ondrej's practice; Dex calls pulling this into the file system 'super smart'. The repo already has docs/ and ADR-0001.
cards.landing: docs/adr and an external-facts file the CLAUDE.md can point to instead of inlining

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the smaller and tighter and more specific you can keep your context window
cards.claim: Context engineering is tied to transformer attention physics and stays relevant until post-transformer architectures: the tighter the context the better, although the floor keeps rising so he does not agonise over each token.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument, no data; also says it was accidentally durable.
cards.landing: Support for shortening CLAUDE.md and keeping phase sessions small

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: put the right tokens into the model, not more tokens
cards.claim: The only primitive is the context window: put the right tokens in, with no wrong or missing information and as small as possible (12-factor 'own your context window'), though caching now makes prompt rewrites costly.
cards.evidence_detail: Recap of 12-factor-agents; at least nine of twelve factors still relevant per Dex.
cards.landing: Basis for trimming CLAUDE.md to what every task needs

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: around 100,000 tokens, about 50% of the context window
cards.claim: The dumb zone originated in a training session with Opus 4.1/4.5: at about 100-120k tokens (around 50% of the window) the group compacted into a doc and started a new session; he calls it training wheels.
cards.evidence_detail: Origin story told in his own words; no benchmark; says you can learn the feel in about three weeks of 70-hour weeks.
cards.landing: Context-budget threshold with the caveat it is a beginner heuristic and model-specific

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I would regularly go up over 200, 300k tokens depending on what I'm doing
cards.claim: He now regularly goes to 200-300k tokens on simple tasks, partly because compaction improved, and if it is not working the move is to start over and reset the problem.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex describes the 'peak of the midwit curve' as strictly obeying the 100k rule; relaxed rule is 'just do what works'.
cards.landing: Relax or tier the one-phase-per-session rule by task risk

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: They had this thing of like context anxiety
cards.claim: Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 realised the window was getting small, cut corners, scrambled and gave up (Calvin French-Owen's exam metaphor), so long contexts hurt through behaviour as well as attention.
cards.evidence_detail: Relayed observation attributed to Calvin French-Owen; Dex adopts it.
cards.landing: Reason to hand off before the end of a window even if quality seems fine

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: adding more coding agents isn't going to solve it
cards.claim: If code review is the bottleneck, more coding agents or token-maxing do not help; find and fix the actual bottleneck, since local efficiency at non-bottleneck stations adds nothing (Goldratt, The Goal).
cards.evidence_detail: Analogy-based argument.
cards.landing: Prioritise review and verification capacity over more orchestration

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Stop playing with your coding agents and get back to work.
cards.claim: Building the thing that builds the thing is seductive; there are inefficiencies that are not bottlenecks, so zoom out and ask whether tooling work addresses the real bottleneck before doing it.
cards.evidence_detail: Office joke at HumanLayer; he says he has argued the other side with bosses about CI speed for years.
cards.landing: Caution on investing in harness tooling (agents, skills, workflow library) without a measured bottleneck

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: much more likely to do it without being told, for sure
cards.claim: Latest-generation agents test and use the browser or computer on their own without being told, so some explicit test instructions can be dropped; Dex agrees with Ondrej's observation.
cards.evidence_detail: Ondrej says new models judge cost, speed and quality themselves after swapping a provider; Dex says computer/browser use improved similarly.
cards.landing: Prune per-model reminders in CLAUDE.md that newer models do unprompted

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You can tell the model how you want it done
cards.claim: Telling the model how narrows the outcome to what you want; leaving it open widens the distribution, risking a bad way or discovering a better one; choose per task.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex frames it as prompting rather than context engineering.
cards.landing: Plan specificity as a dial by risk

cards.source_title: David Ondrej: Agentic Engineering Workflow
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: pull the intuition out earlier on in a way that is like easy
cards.claim: The aim of the workflow is to pull engineers' hard-won intuition into early steps in an easy way, instead of yoloing a 2000-line feature and reviewing everything at the end.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites Jake Nations on intuition; thesis statement.
cards.landing: Why the owner reviews plan, not just PR

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: when you get to 40% start thinking about wrapping it up
cards.claim: Dumb-zone rule of thumb: if you lack experience, at about 40% of the window start wrapping up or do an intentional steer to compaction.
cards.evidence_detail: Primary source of the heuristic; Dex calls it 'training wheels' and 'meant to be a rule of thumb', and tells learners 'shoot for 40%'. No measurement offered.
cards.landing: Context-budget rule in the phase routine; compaction/handoff trigger

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I tell people like shoot for 40% if you're learning.
cards.claim: The 40% figure is for learners; experienced people use less caution because they know what they want.
cards.evidence_detail: Same passage as the dumb-zone rule, restated.
cards.landing: Treat 40% as a default for new/untrusted workflows, revise once the routine has run

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I will regularly blow out to like 60-70% of the context window used.
cards.claim: Experts, and simple tasks, regularly run to 60-70% of the window because a good trajectory can keep improving results, so the 40% is not a hard limit.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says people who have done AI engineering long push to the end of the window; depends on model and task.
cards.landing: Counterweight to a strict one-phase-per-session budget

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: sometimes a good trajectory is worth like you'll actually keep getting better results
cards.claim: A strong early trajectory in the context window can be worth keeping rather than compacting away.
cards.evidence_detail: Offered as explanation for why some experts exceed 40%.
cards.landing: Argues against automatic reset-per-phase when a session is going well

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the only way to know how much context engineering to use on a given problem
cards.claim: You calibrate how much process (research/plan/implement vs just talking to the model) a task needs only through reps of over- and under-doing it; a one-line change does not warrant the whole process.
cards.evidence_detail: Spoken by Dex in the transcript ('you just have to get some reps'); the BigGo summary mis-credits it to the host.
cards.landing: Effort routing: tier process weight by task size

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: talk to Claude for 70 hours a week
cards.claim: Intuition for context and compaction comes from heavy use, not from a framework; there is no better answer.
cards.evidence_detail: Half-joking answer to how to judge whether a compaction is useful.
cards.landing: Reason to encode judgement as explicit checks since a fresh agent lacks the 70 hours

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there will always be a thing that the model can like only kind of get right reliably
cards.claim: Context engineering stays valuable as models improve because the frontier of what is only sometimes right keeps moving outward, and you build great experiences at the edge (idea from the NotebookLM team).
cards.evidence_detail: Credited to a Latent Space episode with the NotebookLM team; Dex says it is still true.
cards.landing: Rationale against dropping the routine as models improve

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Opus 4.5 is AGI uh for people who didn't want to put in the time
cards.claim: Engineers who were good at context engineering were getting the same results from Opus 4.0/4.1 in summer 2025 that others credit to Opus 4.5; the skill, not just the model, sets the ceiling.
cards.evidence_detail: Observations of colleagues; the point is that model upgrades do not remove the need for process.
cards.landing: Cautions against assuming the newest model or higher effort replaces process

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: people who want to build like reliable software and people who want to build a cool demo
cards.claim: Top builders optimise for reliability while public frameworks optimise for demos where 80% correct is fine; enterprise and fintech customers need 'no ship fast and break things'.
cards.evidence_detail: Origin story of 12-factor agents from talking to real builders; customers are 10-20 person startups through 1,000-engineer public companies.
cards.landing: Framing for a money-handling system: reliability-first process

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there's a difference between coding and shipping
cards.claim: Coding is making software work locally; shipping is getting it to prod, fixing it and maintaining it, which AI has not solved; he is annoyed by posts about tokens and parallel sessions rather than shipped, paid-for product.
cards.evidence_detail: Quotes Guillermo Rauch; opinion.
cards.landing: Success measure for phases is shipped and verified in prod, not code volume

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: write working code to like produce working code
cards.claim: The engineer's role changes from writing working code to causing working code to be produced, and the job is finding which parts are high leverage for humans versus AI.
cards.evidence_detail: Prediction for 2026-27, no data.
cards.landing: Role definition for the owner in the phase routine

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: uses AI to write a 10-page document that they didn't read
cards.claim: Slop is any low-effort or derivative output nobody put effort into, most commonly AI text the author did not read.
cards.evidence_detail: Definition given when asked.
cards.landing: Reviewer test: did a human read this artifact

cards.source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: guardrails and guidelines for how to do it
cards.claim: Customer engagements combine workshops and a product so that when Dex leaves the team keeps guardrails and guidelines in the tooling.
cards.evidence_detail: Business description, not a technical claim.
cards.landing: Practice should live in tooling the next session sees, not in a person

cards.source_title: State of the Software Factory (WeAreDevelopers World Congress 2026 NA)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fully autonomous AI coding generates insurmountable slop code and technical debt.
cards.claim: The talk's premise is that fully autonomous AI coding produces unmanageable slop and technical debt.
cards.evidence_detail: Page abstract only (24:07 video); no content from the talk is available.
cards.landing: Consistent with human review gates in the harness
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 - 2026-09-23/25 WeAreDevelopers 'State of the Software Factory'

cards.source_title: State of the Software Factory (WeAreDevelopers World Congress 2026 NA)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: blending deterministic guardrails with strict human oversight
cards.claim: Scaling a software factory safely means combining deterministic guardrails with strict human oversight.
cards.evidence_detail: Page abstract only; specific guardrails and numbers unknown (transcript unavailable).
cards.landing: Points to deterministic enforcement (hooks, scripts, CI) plus human gates; details need the video

gaps: WeAreDevelopers 'State of the Software Factory' (YouTube id -w6RDNBAI0E, 24:07): transcript not available; only the page abstract was carded and marked summarised. Chapters and playback are gated behind a free account; the YouTube video should be read for the talk's actual guardrails and numbers.
